The appellant was the owner of a house in the town of Madras. He was the owner and the appellant was the son of the respondent. The respondent was the owner. The appellant was the sole owner of the house. The respondent filed a suit for possession of the house on the ground that the appellant was in possession of the property as a tenant. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court in appeal held that the appellant had acquired title by adverse possession and that the appellant could not be said to have acquired title by prescription. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the appellant acquired title by virtue of a will executed by his father and that the respondent was entitled to the possession of the appellant. HELD : (i) The appellant was entitled to possession of the suit house. The appellant had no right to possession of it. The respondent had no right in the property. The respondent could not be held to be in possession of it as he had no right of possession. [840 B] (iii) The appellant could have acquired title only by prescription. The Appellate Tribunal, however, took the view that the income tax authorities were not entitled to tax in the hands and the income of Amarchand was not liable. The High Court, however, in a reference under section 66(1) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, held that in the case of a Hindu undivided family, the income of a Hindu joint family was taxable in the name of the family and not in the hands. The firm was assessed to income tax under the Income tax Act, 1922, and the Income tax Officer, on the basis of the decision of the High Court, held that the assessee firm was not a registered firm and that the income tax authorities were not entitled to assess the income of the firm. The assessee firm appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Appellate Tribunal, but the Tribunal held that the firm was not registered as a registered firm under the Income Tax Act, 1922. The Tribunal, however, held that there was no change in the constitution of the firm and that it was not a dissolved firm. The High Court, in reference, held that section 25(4) of the Income tax, Act, 1922 was not applicable to the case. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The High Court was right in holding that the assessee was not a "registered firm" within the meaning of section 2(6) of the Act. [864 D] The expression "registered firm " in section 2(7) of the Indian Income tax Act is not confined to a registered firm as defined in section 2 (6) of that Act. The expression " registered firm " in the Act is not restricted to a registered individual. The expression is not confined only to a registered Hindu undivided family. The expression 'registered firm ' is not confined merely to a registered partnership. The expression, in the context, is not confined in its ordinary sense to a registered society. The expression in the context is not confined, but is confined to a company registered under the Companies Act. [765 D E] The expression ' unregistered firm ' in section 2 of the Income Tax, Act, 1961, is not restricted only to a company which is registered under the Act but is also confined to a firm registered under the Indian Income Tax Act. The appellant, a company, was engaged in the manufacture of a large number of cargo and cargo products. The appellant was employed as a clerk in the respondent company. The respondent company was engaged in work of loading and unloading of cargo and goods. The appellant had to work at the port of Bombay for a period of six months. The appellant, however, was not allowed to work at any port for a period exceeding six months. In the year 1960, the appellant was employed by the respondent company as a clerk. The respondent was paid a sum of Rs. 1,000 per day for the work done by the appellant. The appellant claimed that the respondent was entitled to overtime for the period of six days. The appellant contended that the respondent had been working at the port for a number of hours and that the appellant was entitled to work at a place where the cargo was stored. The respondent contended that the appellant had been working for a number, of hours and had been working only for a number which was less than the number of hours of work. The appellant also contended that the work of loading, unloading and handling of cargo was not of a very serious nature and that the respondent could not be treated as a 'workman ' within the meaning of section 2(s) of the Act. Held, that the appellant could not be said to be a 'workman" within the meaning ofs. 2(s). The definition of 'workman ' in section 2(r) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, is wide enough to include a person who is employed for a period not exceeding six months in any day. The definition of the word 'workman ' is wide enough and includes a person who has been employed for a number not exceeding six days in any day and who has been working for not less than six months in a day. The appellant could not therefore be said to have been employed for more than six months.

In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was in error in holding that the appellant had not established any of the grounds mentioned in section 3 of Act of 1949, and that the appellant could not be said to be a sub tenant. HELD: (i) The High Court was right in holding that section 3 of Bombay Act of 1949 was retrospective. The appellant was a deemed tenant under the Act of 1950. The respondent was a subtenant and the appellant was entitled to be ejected. [864 D] (ii) The appellant was not a sub tenant within the meaning of section 3(1) of the Act. The appellant had not proved that he was in possession of the premises. The respondent had not produced any evidence to show that he was sub tenant. [865 E] (iii) The appellant had failed to establish that he was the sub tenant. The respondent could not be held to be a tenant under section 3 of that Act. [866 D]

The agreement provided that the supply of the water shall be made by the State Government on the terms and conditions specified in the agreement. The agreement was to come into force on the date of the agreement. In the year 1976, the appellant Companies entered upon the agreement with the Government. The appellant Companies entered the agreement on the terms of the agreement and the agreement was to be in force for a period of three years. The agreement further provided that the Government would not be liable to pay any tax or other dues under the agreement. On the question whether the agreement was a contract for the supply or the supply of electricity to the State Government, the Court HELD: (1) The agreement was not a contract for supply of electricity. [851C] (2) The agreement did create a contract for water supply and the supply of energy to the State was to be made by a public authority. The agreement, therefore, did not create a contract. The appellant was a lessee of the mines in the State of Bihar. The lease was for a period of 20 years commencing from April 1, 1949. The lease expired on March 31, 1950. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the lease on the ground that the lease was not for a period exceeding 20 years. The High Court held that the lease in question was for a term of 20 years and not for a term exceeding 20 years and that the lease could not be renewed for a further period of 20 or 20 years. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The lease was not a lease for a term not exceeding 20 years but was a lease for the whole of the lease. The lease in question did not come to an end on the expiry of the lease and the lease was subsisting on the date of the lease, and the lease in favour of the appellant was not a renewed lease.
